items.abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 LLM agents deployed in financial environments must produce outputs that are verifiably correct. Existing benchmarks focus on knowledge retrieval, sentiment analysis, or arithmetic on isolated questions, and do not evaluate the forensic reasoning required to audit large structured datasets across disjointed schemas.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 We introduce two contributions. First, the Pave Interchange Fee Benchmark, a 24-task evaluation suite spanning four levels of forensic complexity, requiring agents to perform multi-file reconciliation, systematic error detection, and financial impact modelling on a synthetic dataset of 50,000 transaction records modelled after real payment processor settlement data. Second, the Adversarial Verification Architecture (Avae 2.0), a three-role multi-agent system in which an Auditor, an Adversarial Verifier, and a Consensus Judge collaborate through a structured rebuttal protocol.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 We evaluate Avae 2.0 against eight state-of-the-art single-agent baselines. Single-agent models perform reasonably on Level 1 aggregation tasks but degrade sharply on Level 3 forensic discovery, with accuracy falling below 55% across all baselines. Avae 2.0 achieves 100% accuracy across all four task levels. We attribute single-agent failure to three recurring patterns: relational blindness, numerical drift, and contextual overload. Our results suggest that architectural constraints, specifically the adversarial consensus requirement, are an important factor in reliability on structured financial reasoning tasks, independent of model scale. The benchmark dataset, evaluation scripts, and ground truth answers are publicly available at github.com/avae-ai/pave-benchmark.
</div></jats:p>
title: Adversarial Consensus Verification for Reliable LLM agents in Financial Forensics: The Pave Interchange Benchmark

items.abstract: <jats:p>There is a pressing need for healthcare conversational agents with domain-specific expertise to ensure the provision of accurate and reliable information tailored to specific medical contexts. Moreover, there is a notable gap in research ensuring the credibility and trustworthiness of the information provided by these healthcare agents, particularly in critical scenarios such as medical emergencies. Pilgrims come from diverse cultural and linguistic backgrounds, often facing difficulties in accessing medical advice and information. Establishing an AI-powered multilingual chatbot can bridge this gap by providing readily available medical guidance and support, contributing to the well-being and safety of pilgrims. In this paper, we present a comprehensive methodology aimed at enhancing the reliability and efficacy of healthcare conversational agents, with a specific focus on addressing the needs of Hajj pilgrims. Our approach leverages domain-specific fine-tuning techniques on a large language model, alongside synthetic data augmentation strategies, to optimize performance in delivering contextually relevant healthcare information by introducing the HajjHealthQA dataset. Additionally, we employ a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) module as a crucial component to validate uncertain generated responses, which improves model performance by 5%. Moreover, we train a secondary AI agent on a well-known health fact-checking dataset and use it to validate medical information in the generated responses. Our approach significantly elevates the chatbot’s accuracy, demonstrating its adaptability to a wide range of pilgrim queries. We evaluate the chatbot’s performance using quantitative and qualitative metrics, highlighting its proficiency in generating accurate responses and achieve competitive results compared to state-of-the-art models, in addition to mitigating the risk of misinformation and providing users with trustworthy health information.</jats:p>
title: Towards Reliable Healthcare LLM Agents: A Case Study for Pilgrims during Hajj
